newsitem.title: USA: Md.'s governor calls for bold income tax cut.
newsitem.headline: Md.'s governor calls for bold income tax cut.

text.p: Maryland Governor Parris Glendening on Tuesday proposed cutting the state's personal income tax rate by 10 percent - from five percent to 4.5 percent - to draw more business to the state and create thousands of new jobs.

The tax cut, to be proposed when the Maryland general assembly convenes in January, would be phased in over three years, beginning in January 1998, Glendening said at a press briefing at Baltimore's World Trade Center.
Glendening said the cut would be the third largest of its kind by any state in the 1990s and would be offset by doubling the state's 36-cents-a-pack cigarette tax.
He said it would be the first time Maryland's income tax rate has been cut to below five percent since the its inception 29 years ago.

The governor said he is certain the tax cut would be paid for and that there will be enough funds available for priorities such as education, public safety, health care for children and environmental protection.
Glendening said the personal income tax rate would be reduced by two percent in 1998, an additional three percent in 1999 and five percent in 2000.

James Brady, Maryland's secretary of business and economic development, said Glendening set the stage for the tax cut when he cut the state's budget by $234 million nearly two years ago upon entering office.
Glendening also worked with the state legislature to set aside $200 million in reserves, Brady said.

A state spokesman said the cost of the tax cut will be covered in later years through "savings from the continued reduction in the size of government, by increases in revenue from an economy stimulated by the tax cut" and new cigarette tax revenues.
Glendening said even after reserves are diverted to pay for the tax cut, the state will continue to hold aside a "rainy day" reserve fund equal to five percent of the state's general fund.
Bond rating agencies have told the state that such reserves are reasonable for a AAA-rated state like Maryland, a the state spokesman said.
Glendening said evidence is mounting that cigarette price hikes reduce smoking by adults and by teens who never pick up the habit as a result of higher costs.
